1.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. The support contract for the council's permit database ends on 31 October next year and extending it is not affordable. Graham Pell, the executive, tells Hannah Okoro that because the project is unavoidable there is no need to compare options or document a business case: the online service named in the mandate should simply be built. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the end of support for the permit database means the council has no choice but to start a project.
It applies it well, because the executive is accountable for the business case and can decide that one is not needed.
It applies it poorly, because even an unavoidable project needs a business case showing that the chosen option gives the best value.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be confirmed by a benefits review before initiation is authorized.
1.w: The principle applies to compulsory and unavoidable projects too: there must be a documented justification for the option chosen (for example replacing only the database versus a full online service), and it must be revalidated throughout (see manual 2.1 and 5.2.3). Dropping the business case because some project is unavoidable applies the principle poorly.

n.0: The deadline explains why some project is needed, but the principle still requires the chosen solution to be justified against the alternatives (manual 2.1).
n.1: The executive owns the business case, but owning it does not mean dispensing with it; principles cannot be tailored away.
n.3: Benefits are confirmed mainly after closure through benefits reviews; before initiation an outline business case is developed and checked, not confirmed.

1.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Hannah Okoro asks the PMO for the lessons report from the council's waste collection app, which went 40% over budget and launched without the contact centre being told. She also arranges a call with a neighbouring council that moved its parking permits online two years ago, and records what she learns in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because the council has run few projects like this and is seeking lessons from its own and other organizations.
Ensure continued business justification, because the waste app overspend shows how actual costs can drift away from a business case.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the waste app went wrong partly because the contact centre was left out.
Tailor to suit the project, because the other council's experience will decide how far the method is adapted for Calderbrook.
1.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start, and when a project is new territory for an organization it is even more important to learn from others, including outside bodies (see manual 2.2). Reviewing lessons reports and consulting people with experience of similar projects is the 'assess previous lessons' activity, recorded in the lessons log (13.4.2).

n.1: Hannah is gathering lessons, not checking whether Permits Online is still desirable, viable and achievable; the overspend is a lesson rather than a test of this project's justification.
n.2: The contact centre point is one of the lessons gathered; the action itself is seeking and recording lessons, not agreeing roles or building relationships.
n.3: Tailoring is agreed in initiation to fit the method to the project; contacting another council for its lessons is learning from experience.

1.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Graham Pell proposes a project board made up of himself and Ruth Abernethy, head of parking services. He says Kestrel Lane Digital is a contractor that can be managed through its contract, and that the council's ICT team can be asked for help when it is needed. How well does this apply the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the council is a thin client and the contract already sets out what Kestrel Lane must deliver.
It applies it well, because a smaller board reduces the time that senior managers spend directing the project.
It applies it poorly, because the head of parking services should be the executive, as she will run the service.
It applies it poorly, because the supplier interest of Kestrel Lane and the ICT team is not represented on the board.
1.w: The principle requires a project management team that engages the business, user and supplier interests, reflected in the make-up of the project board (see manual 2.3 and 6.2.1). Kestrel Lane and the council's ICT team supply the products, so a senior supplier role is needed; a contract does not replace supplier representation in decision-making.

n.0: A thin client model means the supplier does much of the work, which makes supplier representation more important; the contract does not give the supplier a voice in direction.
n.1: Board size should be proportionate, but leaving out one of the three project interests is not a valid way to reduce the burden.
n.2: Ruth Abernethy will use and run the service, which suits the senior user role; Graham Pell holds the budget and is named as accountable in the mandate, which suits the executive role.

1.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. The plan has four stages: initiation, discovery and alpha, a private beta in the Old Town ward, and a public beta with migration. To reduce the number of board meetings, Graham Pell suggests merging the private and public beta into one 28-week stage. The private beta is the first time real permits will be issued online. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because longer stages reduce the burden on senior management and the project still has more than two stages.
It applies it well, because the board can still be told about problems in the private beta through exception reports.
It applies it poorly, because each delivery stage should be the same length so that progress can be compared between stages.
It applies it poorly, because the end of the private beta is a key point to review real-user results before launching borough-wide.
1.w: Stages give the board decision points at which to judge whether to commit further, and shorter stages give more control (see manual 2.4). The end of the private beta is the natural point to decide, on evidence from real users and with a very low appetite for data and accessibility risk, whether to launch borough-wide and migrate every permit. Merging the stages removes that decision point.

n.0: It is true that longer stages reduce the board's burden and that two stages is the minimum, but the risk of going live borough-wide calls for a decision point after the private beta.
n.1: Exception reports deal with forecast tolerance breaches; they do not give the planned go or no-go decision that a stage boundary provides.
n.2: Stage length depends on the planning horizon, risk and decision points; there is no rule that stages must be of equal length.

1.q: Matching set (business case). Hannah Okoro is preparing the full business case for Permits Online. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: The project will run for 44 weeks from the start of initiation, and its benefits will be realized over the two years after launch.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Time
Costs
1.w: The time heading records the period over which the project runs and the period over which its benefits are expected to be realized (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.0: Reasons explain why the project is needed and how it supports business objectives, not how long the project and its benefits will take.
n.1: Expected benefits states the measurable improvements themselves; when they will be realized is recorded under time.
n.3: Costs covers project costs and ongoing running costs with their funding, not durations.

1.q: Matching set (business case). Hannah Okoro is preparing the full business case for Permits Online. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: Support for the current permit database ends on 31 October next year, and the corporate plan commits the council to services that are digital by preference.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Time
Costs
1.w: The reasons heading explains why the project is needed and how it enables the organization's business objectives, here the end of support and the corporate plan's digital commitment (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.1: These are the drivers for the project, not measurable improvements that it will produce.
n.2: No duration or period of benefits realization is given; these explain why the project is needed.
n.3: No cost or funding information is given.

1.q: Matching set (business case). Hannah Okoro is preparing the full business case for Permits Online. Which heading of the business case should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Kestrel Lane will charge £48,000 a year to host and support the live service, funded from the parking services budget.
o: Reasons
Expected benefits
Time
Costs
1.w: The costs heading includes ongoing operations and maintenance costs as well as project costs, together with how they will be funded (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.0: A running charge is not a reason for undertaking the project.
n.1: A charge is a cost of the investment, not an improvement it delivers.
n.2: The yearly charge is a cost of running the product; the time heading records the duration of the project and of benefits realization.

1.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Permits Online is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Graham Pell
Ruth Abernethy
Siobhan Kerr
Priya Lal
1.w: Graham Pell is the budget holder for parking services and is named in the mandate as accountable for Permits Online. The executive is the single point of accountability for the project, secures its funding and owns the business case (manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.1: Ruth Abernethy runs the service that will use the products, which suits the senior user role; she does not hold the budget or the accountability named in the mandate.
n.2: Siobhan Kerr leads the supplier and represents its interests, which suits the senior supplier role; the executive represents the council's business interest.
n.3: Priya Lal has no role in parking services and no budget; her independent review role suits assurance.

1.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Permits Online is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior supplier.
o: Graham Pell
Ruth Abernethy
Siobhan Kerr
Priya Lal
1.w: Siobhan Kerr is Kestrel Lane's delivery director, accountable for the agency's staff, its contract and the technical quality of what it builds. The senior supplier represents those delivering the products, commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality of the supplier's products (manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Graham Pell is best placed as executive, holding the budget and named as accountable; he does not lead the organization delivering the products.
n.1: Ruth Abernethy runs the service that will use the products, so she represents users rather than suppliers.
n.3: Priya Lal reviews digital projects for the council; she does not lead the supplier or commit its staff.

1.q: Matching set (organizing). The project management team for Permits Online is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Project assurance, carried out by someone the board appoints to review the project on its behalf.
o: Graham Pell
Ruth Abernethy
Siobhan Kerr
Priya Lal
1.w: Project assurance must be independent of the project manager and is carried out for the board. Priya Lal already reviews digital projects against the council's service standard and has no role in parking services, so she can give the board an independent view (manual 6.2.4).

n.0: Graham Pell is best suited to be the executive, a board member, rather than someone the board appoints to assure the project for it.
n.1: Ruth Abernethy runs the service that the project changes and is best suited to be the senior user, a board member.
n.2: Siobhan Kerr is accountable for Kestrel Lane's delivery and suits the senior supplier role; she cannot give an independent view of her own agency's work.

1.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Because the ICT team is supporting three other projects, the council tax integration may be finished late, which would delay the start of the private beta.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
1.w: A risk description sets out the cause (the ICT team's other commitments), the uncertain event (late integration) and the effect on objectives (a delayed private beta) (see manual 9.2.1 and 9.5).

n.0: No person is named; the statement describes what the risk is.
n.2: No timing is given for when the risk might occur.
n.3: No action or person carrying it out is named; this is the cause, event and effect.

1.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The risk could occur in weeks 6 to 10 of the discovery and alpha stage, when the integration is due to be built.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
1.w: Proximity records how close in time the risk is likely to occur (see manual 9.5).

n.0: No person is named; this states when the risk might occur.
n.1: This states when the risk might occur, not its cause, event and effect.
n.3: No agreed action or person carrying it out is named.

1.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Alan Briggs, ICT infrastructure manager, is responsible for managing this risk and its response.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
1.w: The risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for managing a risk and responding to it; a risk action owner carries out specific agreed actions on the owner's behalf (see manual 9.2 and the risk register composition).

n.1: This names who manages the risk, not what the risk is.
n.2: No timing is given for when the risk might occur.
n.3: A risk action owner carries out a specific agreed action for the risk owner; Alan Briggs is responsible for managing the risk as a whole.

1.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 1 of 3: Enter a new request for change from the Old Town Residents' Association in the issue register.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
1.w: Project support administers the issue and change control procedures by maintaining the issue register (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.0: The senior user decides on escalated issues; keeping the register is administration.
n.1: The project manager runs the issue procedure and keeps the register when there is no project support; here project support is in place.
n.2: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not keep the issue register.

1.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 2 of 3: Carry out the agreed rework of the payment page within the team's current work package after it failed an accessibility check.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
1.w: Team managers implement corrective actions within their work packages (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.0: The senior user decides on escalated issues; the rework itself is done by the team.
n.1: The project manager authorizes corrective action and creates new work packages where needed, but carrying out rework within the current work package falls to the team manager.
n.3: Project support administers the issue register; it does not rework products.

1.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 3 of 3: Decide on an escalated request for change, with a focus on protecting the expected cut in processing time.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
1.w: When issues are escalated, the senior user makes decisions with a focus on safeguarding the expected benefits (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.1: The project manager handles issues within delegated authority; an escalated request is decided above that level, where the senior user protects the expected benefits.
n.2: Team managers implement actions; they do not decide escalated issues.
n.3: Project support records the decision in the issue register; it does not make it.

1.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Hannah Okoro meets Graham Pell, Ruth Abernethy and Siobhan Kerr to agree what the project will deliver. Together they draft the project product description, including the users' quality expectations and the go-live conditions as acceptance criteria. Is this an appropriate application of the 'prepare the outline business case' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the executive, senior user and senior supplier are consulted to define what the project will deliver.
Yes, because the outline business case must contain the detailed costs from the project product description.
No, because the project product description is created in initiation as part of preparing the project plan.
No, because the senior supplier should not be involved until the project has been authorized by the board.
1.w: In 'prepare the outline business case' the project manager consults the executive, senior user and senior supplier to understand what the project is to deliver and creates the project product description, including the quality expectations and acceptance criteria (see manual 13.4.3).

n.1: The outline business case is high level at this point; detailed costs come from the project plan in initiation.
n.2: The project product description is created in starting up a project; it is then used in initiation and when closing the project.
n.3: The senior supplier is consulted in starting up so that what is to be delivered is understood from the supplier side too.

1.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. The chief executive's office has appointed Graham Pell as executive. Graham is now choosing the senior user and senior supplier and agreeing who will provide project assurance. Which role is accountable for the 'appoint the project management team' activity?
o: The executive, Graham Pell, who is choosing the other members of the board.
The project manager, Hannah Okoro, who will lead the project team day to day.
The project board, once all of its members have been appointed.
The business layer, here the chief executive's office that commissioned the project.
1.w: In the recommended RACI for 'appoint the project management team', the business layer is accountable and the executive is responsible for making the appointments; the project manager is not involved (see manual 13.4.4 and table 13.2).

n.0: Graham Pell is responsible for carrying out the appointments; accountability for them sits with the business layer.
n.1: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
n.2: The board cannot be accountable for appointing itself; the business layer that commissions the project is accountable.

1.q: Permits Online is in the 'starting up a project' process. Worried about the fixed date of 31 October, Hannah Okoro asks Kestrel Lane to start building prototype screens straight away, before the project brief has been approved, so that the alpha stage can be shortened later. Is this an effective way to carry out starting up a project, and why?
o: Yes, because early prototypes help to show whether the project is viable before initiation is authorized.
Yes, because Kestrel Lane works iteratively and the project approach allows design work to begin early.
No, because starting up should do the minimum needed to decide whether initiation is worthwhile.
No, because the council's ICT team, not Kestrel Lane, should build any prototypes for the project.
1.w: Starting up a project is deliberately light: it does the minimum needed to decide whether there is a viable and worthwhile project to initiate, and it prevents resources being committed before that decision (see manual 13.1). Building prototypes is delivery work and should wait until the board has authorized it.

n.0: Viability at this point is judged from the outline business case and project brief, not from delivery work done before any authorization.
n.1: The project approach describes how the work will be delivered once authorized; it does not allow delivery to start before initiation.
n.3: Who builds the prototypes is not the problem: Kestrel Lane is the appointed supplier, but no delivery work should start before authorization.

1.q: The project brief and initiation stage plan for Permits Online have been sent to the board. Graham Pell, Ruth Abernethy and Siobhan Kerr each review them and agree by email that initiation should go ahead, without holding a meeting. Graham then emails Hannah Okoro a written instruction to start the six-week initiation stage. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize initiation' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager may begin initiation as soon as the project brief is complete.
Yes, because all board members agreed and the executive gave the project manager a documented instruction.
No, because initiation must be authorized at a formal board meeting at which minutes are taken.
No, because the business layer, not the project board, authorizes the start of the initiation stage.
1.w: Authorize initiation can be done with or without a formal meeting, as long as all board members agree and the project manager receives a documented instruction from the executive (see manual 14.4.1).

n.0: The project manager needs the board's authority to initiate; completing the brief leads to the request, not the start.
n.2: A formal meeting is not required for this decision.
n.3: Authorizing initiation is a project board decision in directing a project; the business layer provides the mandate.

1.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Hannah Okoro and Tom Achebe draft the work package description for the eligibility checks together. They agree time and cost tolerances, a scope tolerance on optional features, checkpoint reports after each sprint review and how finished products will be handed over. Tom confirms his team can deliver it before Hannah authorizes the work. Is this an appropriate application of the 'authorize a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager sets the tolerances for the work package and the project manager records them.
Yes, because the project manager co-creates the work package with the team manager and confirms acceptance.
No, because the work package description should also set a benefits tolerance for processing time.
No, because work packages should be authorized by the project board as part of approving the stage plan.
1.w: In 'authorize a work package' the project manager defines the work package, co-creates and reviews it with the team manager, confirms that the team manager accepts it and then authorizes the work (see manual 16.4.1). Work package tolerances cover scope, cost and time.

n.0: The project manager sets work package tolerances; the team manager agrees to work within them.
n.2: Benefits and quality tolerances are not set in a work package description; its tolerances are scope, cost and time.
n.3: The board approves stage plans; authorizing work packages within the stage is the project manager's activity in controlling a stage.

1.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. While evaluating stage status, Hannah Okoro finds that the telephone assisted route is behind schedule but still within stage tolerance. She moves two Kestrel Lane developers onto the work through an amended work package. Which role is accountable for the 'take corrective action' activity?
o: The executive.
The project manager.
The team manager.
Project support.
1.w: In the recommended RACI for 'take corrective action', the executive is accountable, the project manager is responsible for selecting and triggering the action, and project support is informed (see manual 16.4.6 and table 16.2).

n.1: The project manager is responsible for taking the corrective action; accountability for the activity sits with the executive.
n.2: The team manager carries out the amended work package but is not accountable for the activity.
n.3: Project support is informed of corrective action, not accountable for it.

1.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage and is forecast to finish within its tolerances. Dev Mistry tells Hannah Okoro that contact centre staff have not been briefed on the online service and are giving residents wrong advice. Without recording or assessing the problem, Hannah sends the board an exception report the same day. Is this an effective way to carry out controlling a stage, and why?
o: Yes, because the waste app lesson shows that contact centre problems must go straight to the board.
Yes, because the board should be alerted as early as possible to anything affecting residents.
No, because the issue should be captured and assessed first, and no stage tolerance breach is forecast.
No, because contact centre problems are business as usual and so lie outside the project's control.
1.w: In 'capture issues and risks' each issue is registered and assessed before a course of action is chosen (see manual 16.4.5). An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage tolerance (16.4.7); here the stage is within tolerance, so the project manager should handle the problem, for example by arranging briefings, and report it in the next highlight report.

n.0: The lesson is about telling the contact centre, which this problem shows is needed; it does not change how issues are escalated.
n.1: Alerting the board early applies to forecast exceptions; issues within tolerance are handled by the project manager.
n.3: Preparing the contact centre for the new service is part of the project's communication and change work, so this is a project issue.

1.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. Tom Achebe receives the draft work package for the council tax integration interface. It relies on Alan Briggs's ICT team, who are free for two days a week, so the planned four sprints are not achievable. Before agreeing to it, Tom discusses the timescale and the dependency with Hannah Okoro, and they agree a revised work package. Is this an appropriate application of the 'accept a work package' activity, and why?
o: Yes, because the team manager sets the tolerances for the work package once it has been accepted.
Yes, because the team manager agrees with the project manager what will be delivered and whether it is achievable.
No, because the team manager should accept the work package as authorized and report problems in checkpoints.
No, because Tom Achebe should take the dependency on the ICT team to the project board to resolve.
1.w: In 'accept a work package' the team manager agrees with the project manager what is to be delivered, the reporting requirements, constraints and procedures, and confirms that it is achievable before committing to it (see manual 17.4.1).

n.0: The project manager sets work package tolerances; the team manager agrees to work within them.
n.2: Acceptance is an agreement, not a formality; problems known at the start should be resolved before the team manager commits.
n.3: The team manager works with the project manager, not the board; the board is not involved in managing product delivery.

2.q: Tarnside College's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'starting up a project' process. In the outline business case, Leah Whitfield compares leaving the warehouse empty, converting it for welding and electrical courses without the nacelle rig, and building the full centre. For each option she weighs the grant, the employers' apprentice pledges and the risk of grant clawback against the cost to the college. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Focus on products, because each option is defined by the products it would deliver, such as the welding bays and the nacelle rig.
Manage by exception, because the governors have limited spending on the centre to 3% above the approved budget.
Ensure continued business justification, because the options are compared to find the best balance of benefits, costs and risks.
Learn from experience, because the lab refurbishment showed that the college must plan its capital projects with more care.
2.w: Ensure continued business justification: there must be a justifiable reason for the project, documented in a business case, and the chosen option should give the best overall value. Comparing doing nothing, doing the minimum and doing more than the minimum, and weighing benefits against costs and risks, is how that justification is developed (see manual 2.1 and 5.3.1).

n.0: The options are described by what they deliver, but the purpose of the comparison is to justify the investment, not to define products and their quality requirements.
n.1: The 3% limit is a tolerance, which belongs to manage by exception; the action here is comparing options to justify the investment.
n.3: No previous lessons are being sought or applied in this action; Leah is analysing business options.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. In starting up, Leah Whitfield recorded the lab refurbishment lessons in the lessons log, including that changes had been agreed on site without anyone checking the budget. To keep the work moving, Mark Ostrowski now proposes that the contractor's site manager and Craig Dunmore agree design changes at weekly site meetings and tell Leah afterwards. How well does this apply the 'learn from experience' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the lessons log was created in starting up, as the 'assess previous lessons' activity recommends.
It applies it well, because Craig Dunmore has managed many small works contracts and understands the college's budgets.
It applies it poorly, because the lessons log should be set up in initiation, once the board has authorized the project.
It applies it poorly, because the lessons were recorded but the proposal repeats the same mistake rather than acting on it.
2.w: Learn from experience means lessons are sought, recorded and acted on throughout the project (see manual 2.2). The lab refurbishment showed the danger of agreeing changes on site without checking the budget; agreeing design changes at site meetings and telling the project manager afterwards repeats it, so the lesson has been recorded but not applied.

n.0: Creating the lessons log in starting up is correct, but recording lessons is not enough: this proposal repeats the very mistake the lessons warned about.
n.1: Craig's experience does not change the lesson that site changes need their cost checked before they are agreed.
n.2: The lessons log is created in starting up a project ('assess previous lessons'), so recording the lessons then was correct.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Leah Whitfield sets up a group that meets every six weeks, bringing together Ade Okafor of Brackmoor Offshore Wind, the other wind operator, Sunita Rao and Bethany Cole. Its purpose is for the employers and the college to understand each other's priorities, agree who contacts whom on apprentice matters and keep the employers engaged as the design develops. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the project is building relationships with key external stakeholders.
Focus on products, because the group will set the quality specifications for the nacelle rig before it is ordered.
Ensure continued business justification, because the employers' pledges are the main source of the project's benefits.
Learn from experience, because the wind operators already train apprentices and can pass on lessons from their own centres.
2.w: The principle now covers relationships as well as roles: the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). A regular group that helps the employers and the college understand each other and agree who contacts whom does exactly that.

n.1: The group exists to build understanding and agree contacts, not to write product descriptions or quality specifications.
n.2: The pledges matter to the business case, but the action described is building relationships, not checking that the project is still justified.
n.3: Nothing in the group's purpose is about seeking or recording lessons; it is about relationships and engagement.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is at the end of the detailed design and procurement stage, and the design-and-build contract is about to be signed. To save board time, Mark Ostrowski proposes treating stages 3, 4 and 5 as a single 13-month stage running to the opening day, because the contractor's programme covers all of that work. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because longer stages reduce the burden on senior managers, and the contractor's programme has been agreed.
It applies it well, because the board will still receive highlight reports and can step in if a problem arises.
It applies it poorly, because a 13-month stage removes the points where the board reviews viability before committing more.
It applies it poorly, because commissioning and handover should be planned as part of a separate closing stage.
2.w: Manage by stages gives the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability before authorizing the next stage; shorter stages give more control, longer ones less burden (see manual 2.4). Merging the structural, fit-out and handover stages leaves no point between signing the contract and opening day at which the board decides whether to continue, despite the tight cost limit.

n.0: Stage length is a trade-off, but on a large build with a 3% cost limit and a fixed date, one 13-month stage gives up too much control; the contractor's programme does not replace board decision points.
n.1: Highlight reports keep the board informed, but they are not decision points at which the board reviews viability and authorizes the next commitment.
n.3: Closing a project is not a stage; it is the last part of the final stage, so commissioning and handover cannot move into a closing stage.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The governors' limit of 3% above the approved budget and the fixed September opening are recorded as project tolerances. The board sets cost and time tolerances for each stage, Leah Whitfield agrees to raise an exception report as soon as a stage is forecast to go beyond them, and Mark Ostrowski will refer any forecast beyond the project tolerances to the governors. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board sets separate cost and time tolerances for each of the five stages.
Ensure continued business justification, because a forecast overspend beyond 3% would threaten the college's reserves.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Leah and Mark each have a defined part in escalating problems.
Manage by exception, because each level has limits of delegated authority and forecast breaches are escalated to the next level.
2.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances, with escalation to the next level as soon as a breach is forecast: the business layer sets project tolerances, the board stage tolerances, and exceptions go upwards (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.1).

n.0: Tolerances are set per stage, but setting limits of authority and escalating forecast breaches is manage by exception.
n.1: An overspend would affect justification, but the arrangement described sets limits of delegated authority and escalation routes.
n.2: Roles are involved, but the core of the arrangement is tolerances at each level and escalation when they are forecast to be exceeded.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before the architect starts the detailed design, Leah Whitfield arranges for Bethany Cole, Craig Dunmore and the architect to write the product description for the welding bays together. It sets out what each bay contains, the fume extraction performance it must achieve and who will review and approve it. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because Craig Dunmore holds a health and safety qualification and can approve the fume extraction design.
It applies it well, because defining each product and its quality requirements before design guides the work and avoids waste.
It applies it poorly, because product descriptions should be written by the supplier once the contract has been awarded.
It applies it poorly, because the vice principal's request for 30 bays must be decided before any product description is written.
2.w: Focus on products means defining products and their quality expectations before the work, so that the project is output-oriented and does no more than needed; product descriptions give purpose, composition, quality specifications and approval responsibilities, and co-creating them with users helps adoption (see manual 2.6 and 3.5.1).

n.0: Who approves is set out in the product description itself; Craig's qualification does not explain why defining the product first is good practice.
n.2: Product descriptions are prepared when planning, with input from users and suppliers; waiting for the contractor would leave the design without agreed requirements.
n.3: A request for change is handled through issue control; it does not stop the bays being described now, and the description can be updated if a change is approved.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield proposes calling the project board the 'Skills Centre Steering Group', as the college names its capital project boards, using the college's capital project report template for highlight reports, and adding a site safety section to every highlight report, as one governor has asked. How well does this apply the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the method can use the college's terms and formats and report the risks that matter here.
It applies it well, because tailoring lets the college set aside the principles that do not suit a building project.
It applies it poorly, because PRINCE2 names should be kept so that everyone can recognize the roles and products.
It applies it poorly, because tailoring is decided by the business layer before the project manager is appointed.
2.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's environment and risk: terminology can follow the organization's own, management products can take different formats, and controls such as reporting are shaped to the project's needs, here the safety risk next to the student entrance (see manual 2.7). The decisions are documented in the PID for the board to approve.

n.1: Principles cannot be tailored away; tailoring adapts processes, practices, roles, products and terminology.
n.2: Using the organization's own terminology is a recognized form of tailoring.
n.3: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiation, and the board approves the result in the PID.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. The curriculum team designs courses in the main college building, while the contractor's site team, the Danish rig installers and Leah Whitfield, who works three days a week, are seldom on site together. Misunderstandings about room layouts are growing. Leah sets up a fortnightly site walk-round and lunch for Bethany Cole, the site manager and the installers, with a shared online board for questions in between. Is this an appropriate approach to leading the team, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager's role is to instruct each team on how its tasks should be carried out.
Yes, because regular purposeful contact builds trust and social cohesion between groups that rarely work together.
No, because the curriculum team belongs to the user community and so is not part of the project team.
No, because the contractor's staff work for their own company and so are outside Leah's leadership.
2.w: Bringing teams together means optimizing people's time and building social cohesion: people meeting purposefully and regularly, building trust across project silos; teams that are not co-located need deliberate methods to achieve this (see manual 3.3.3).

n.0: Instructing tasks is management; the action here is building trust and cohesion between groups, which is leadership.
n.2: People who use the products contribute to the project; the curriculum team is doing project work on the courses.
n.3: Leading across organizational boundaries is part of leading project teams; it calls for cultural intelligence, not exclusion.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Mark Ostrowski proposes that Craig Dunmore's estates team administer the design-and-build contract and check the contractor's monthly valuations, as they manage the college's small works contracts. Leah Whitfield notes that nobody in the team has handled a contract above £200,000, while Hamish Grant's firm checks valuations on large projects. Is this an appropriate approach to building the team, and why?
o: Yes, because the estates team will look after the building once it opens and so should own the contract.
Yes, because the college is acting as a thick client and should do most of the project work itself.
No, because contract administration is a project support task and so cannot be given to user representatives.
No, because roles should match capability, and the gap should be closed by upskilling or by giving the work to others.
2.w: Roles should reflect capability, authority and availability; the project manager identifies competency gaps and mitigates them, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibilities to more suitable people, such as the cost consultant who already checks valuations (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Looking after the building later does not give the team the capability to administer a large contract now.
n.1: A thick client does much of the work itself, but roles should still go to people with the capability to fill them.
n.2: Contract tasks are not reserved to project support; the problem is the capability gap, not who the team represents.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Tenders show the budget is tight, and Mark Ostrowski suggests replacing the nacelle rig with a cheaper computer simulator. Before any recommendation goes to the board, Leah Whitfield meets Ade Okafor and the other wind operator to understand what their apprentices must be able to do on a real rig and how a simulator would affect their pledges. Is this an appropriate way to lead change with the people affected, and why?
o: Yes, because the wind operators are key influencers whose pledges rest on the rig, so their needs should shape the decision.
Yes, because the employers are paying for the rig and so have the authority to approve or reject the change.
No, because employers outside the college are not project stakeholders and can be informed after the board has decided.
No, because the change is a request for change, which the board decides without consulting stakeholders.
2.w: Stakeholder engagement means identifying stakeholders and key influencers and building relationships so that all impacted areas are involved as the project progresses (see manual 3.2.2). The wind operators say the rig is the main reason they are committing apprentices, so their needs should shape any recommendation.

n.1: The rig is funded by the grant and college reserves; the employers have influence, not authority over project decisions.
n.2: Stakeholders include organizations outside the business that can affect or be affected by the project; the employers are key ones.
n.3: Assessing a change is best done cooperatively; understanding its effect on stakeholders informs the recommendation to the board.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Three of the college's current electrical instructors, who will move into the new centre, keep objecting to the planned teaching timetable and have stopped attending design workshops. Sunita Rao suggests leaving them out of the remaining workshops so that decisions can be made faster. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because co-creation works best with people who support the change and will promote it to others.
Yes, because the instructors' line manager can direct them to accept the timetable once the centre opens.
No, because their resistance shows where engagement is needed, so the reasons behind it should be explored.
No, because each instructor is a senior user and must approve the course timetable before the centre opens.
2.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication and engagement should be focused: find out why people resist rather than sidelining them, and involve users in co-creating the ways of working they will adopt (see manual 3.2 and 3.4).

n.0: Co-creation involves users and key influencers, including doubters; excluding them makes adoption less likely.
n.1: Directing people to comply does not deal with the cause of resistance or help them move to the target state.
n.3: The instructors are users, but they do not hold the senior user role; Sunita Rao represents the users on the board.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is about to start the asbestos removal and strip-out. Site traffic will use a new gate, and the student pedestrian route will move for four months. About 1,800 students aged 16 to 18 use the main campus each day, and many arrive by bus. Leah Whitfield is updating the communication management approach. Which action BEST applies it?
o: Ask the main contractor to post notices on the site hoarding, as it is responsible for safety on its own site.
Plan messages for students, parents and bus operators through channels they use, with a way to raise concerns.
Add the route change to the next highlight report, so that the board and governors know about it first.
Send one email to all students and staff from the principal on the day before the strip-out starts.
2.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder group, based on stakeholder analysis of who is affected (see manual 3.4). Students, parents and bus operators are directly affected by the moved route, so messages should reach them through suitable channels before and during the work, with a way to respond.

n.0: Site notices reach people who are already at the site; they do not plan messages for each affected group or allow feedback.
n.2: The highlight report informs the board about stage status; it does not reach the students and others who are affected.
n.3: A single late message with no route for feedback does not give a controlled, two-way flow of information.

2.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield drafts this entry for the communication management approach: 'Rachel Tse, sustainability manager: reports on the climate targets to the governors and the combined authority; strong influence on grant compliance scoring; worried that the heat pumps could be cut to save money.' Under which heading should this entry be recorded, and why?
o: Communications schedule and procedures, because it sets out how Rachel will report to the combined authority.
Supporting tools and techniques, because Rachel uses reporting tools to track the climate emergency targets.
Stakeholder analysis, because it records who is affected by or can influence the project and their current views.
Resources, because Rachel's time is needed for the project's communication activities on sustainability.
2.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is impacted by the project's outcome or delivery and who can influence its success or failure, with their interests and concerns (see manual 3.4). Rachel's role, influence on grant scoring and concern about the heat pumps belong there; the schedule and procedures then plan the messages for her.

n.0: The entry does not set out when or how messages will be sent; it describes Rachel's interest, influence and position.
n.1: No tool or platform for communication is described; the entry is about a stakeholder.
n.3: The entry does not commit Rachel's time to communication work; it analyses her as a stakeholder.

2.q: Matching set (business case). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Which management product, or heading of the business case, should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Sunita Rao's team will count apprentice enrolments each September for three years after opening and report the figures at planned benefits reviews.
o: Business case: expected benefits
Benefits management approach
Business case: costs
Sustainability management approach
2.w: The benefits management approach defines the benefits management actions and benefits reviews, including how and when benefits are measured and who is responsible, so that realization can be confirmed after the project (manual 5.5 and 5.3.1).

n.0: The expected benefits heading states the measurable benefits themselves; the measurement actions, timing and reviews belong in the benefits management approach.
n.2: No cost is described; this is how and when a benefit will be measured and reviewed.
n.3: Apprentice numbers are a benefit measure, not a sustainability performance target.

2.q: Matching set (business case). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Which management product, or heading of the business case, should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: The heat pumps and solar panels will add £38,000 a year to the centre's running and maintenance costs, met from the estates budget.
o: Business case: expected benefits
Benefits management approach
Business case: costs
Sustainability management approach
2.w: The costs heading of the business case covers project costs and the ongoing operations and maintenance costs of the products, with their funding arrangements (business case composition, manual chapter 5).

n.0: This is a cost of owning the products, not an improvement they bring.
n.1: A running cost is not a benefits management action or review.
n.3: The sustainability management approach sets the actions, reviews and controls for sustainability targets; the running cost of the equipment and its funding belong under costs.

2.q: Matching set (business case). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Which management product, or heading of the business case, should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: Construction waste diverted from landfill will be checked monthly from the contractor's waste records, with a tolerance of two percentage points below the 90% target.
o: Business case: expected benefits
Benefits management approach
Business case: costs
Sustainability management approach
2.w: Sustainability performance targets and tolerances are documented in the sustainability management approach, which defines the actions, reviews and controls needed to achieve them (manual 5.2.2).

n.0: Diverting waste is a sustainability target for the work, not an expected benefit of the centre.
n.1: Waste diversion is a sustainability target, not one of the project's benefits; its tolerance and checks belong in the sustainability management approach.
n.2: No cost is described; this is a target, a tolerance and a control.

2.q: Matching set (organizing). Greystack Build Ltd has won the design-and-build contract, and the project board for Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre is being confirmed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Paul Kettering
Mark Ostrowski
Owen Pryce
Sunita Rao
2.w: Mark Ostrowski controls the college budget and reserves that part-fund the project and has led a major capital project. The executive is the single point of accountability, owns the business case and secures funding (manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.0: Paul Kettering is a governor and chairs the finance and resources committee, which belongs to the business layer that sets project tolerances; he is not part of the college's management with the budget to commit.
n.2: Owen Pryce represents the contractor, which suits the senior supplier role; the executive represents the college's business interest.
n.3: Sunita Rao is responsible for the apprenticeship programmes that will use the centre, which suits the senior user role.

2.q: Matching set (organizing). Greystack Build Ltd has won the design-and-build contract, and the project board for Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre is being confirmed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior user.
o: Paul Kettering
Mark Ostrowski
Owen Pryce
Sunita Rao
2.w: Sunita Rao is responsible for the apprenticeship programmes that will run in the centre and for recruiting its instructors. The senior user represents those who will use the products, specifies the benefits and is responsible for showing that forecast benefits are on track and for their realization after closure (manual 6.2.4.2 and appendix B).

n.0: Paul Kettering is a governor in the business layer and will not use the centre's products.
n.1: Mark Ostrowski holds the budget and accountability for value, which suits the executive role.
n.2: Owen Pryce represents the organization delivering the building, not the people who will use it.

2.q: Matching set (organizing). Greystack Build Ltd has won the design-and-build contract, and the project board for Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre is being confirmed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual would be most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Senior supplier.
o: Paul Kettering
Mark Ostrowski
Owen Pryce
Sunita Rao
2.w: Owen Pryce is contracts director at Greystack Build, which will design and build the centre. The senior supplier represents those delivering the products, commits supplier resources and is accountable for the quality of supplier products (manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.0: Paul Kettering is a governor and a retired construction director; he does not represent or commit any supplier's resources.
n.1: Mark Ostrowski represents the college's business interest as executive.
n.3: Sunita Rao represents the users of the centre.

2.q: Matching set (plans). Leah Whitfield is writing the work package description for the asbestos removal in stage 3, to be carried out by a licensed subcontractor. Under which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 1 of 3: Site vehicles must not cross the student pedestrian route, and no removal work may take place while students are arriving or leaving.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
2.w: Constraints in a work package description cover restrictions on how the work is done, such as permitted hours, safety and security requirements (plans practice, work package description composition, manual chapter 7).

n.0: These are restrictions on when and where work may happen, not the methods to be used for removal.
n.2: References list the documents the work package draws on, such as higher-level plans; these are restrictions.
n.3: No target or permitted deviation for time, cost or scope is stated.

2.q: Matching set (plans). Leah Whitfield is writing the work package description for the asbestos removal in stage 3, to be carried out by a licensed subcontractor. Under which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 2 of 3: Complete the removal in five weeks at a cost of £140,000, plus or minus three days and £7,000.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
2.w: A work package description sets the targets and the time, cost and scope tolerances within which the team manager works; benefits and quality tolerances are not set at this level (manual 11.2.1).

n.0: Duration, cost and permitted deviation are targets and tolerances, not techniques.
n.1: These are targets with permitted deviations rather than restrictions on how the work is done.
n.2: Figures for time and cost with a permitted deviation are tolerances, not references to other documents.

2.q: Matching set (plans). Leah Whitfield is writing the work package description for the asbestos removal in stage 3, to be carried out by a licensed subcontractor. Under which heading of the work package description should each piece of information be recorded? Statement 3 of 3: The stage 3 plan, the asbestos survey report and the product description for the cleared warehouse.
o: Techniques and procedures
Constraints
References
Targets and tolerances
2.w: References identify the documents the work package relies on, such as the stage plan it comes from and related product descriptions (plans practice, work package description composition, manual chapter 7).

n.0: These are documents to refer to, not the methods the subcontractor will use.
n.1: No restriction on the work is described; these are source documents.
n.3: No time, cost or scope targets are given.
